item.title: This tiny retro handheld makes me wish translucent tech had never gone away
item.itunes:title: This tiny retro handheld makes me wish translucent tech had never gone away
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I'm a sucker for gaming handhelds, especially if they have some sort of retro appeal to them, so when an email from the team at Arduview landed in my inbox, I knew I needed to check out the portable. In a homage to the 90s and early-2000s, the tiny Arduview is entirely translucent, similar to ModRetro's M64. It also takes things to another level because its actual display is see-through. Wild, right?

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The team behind the handheld calls the Arduview the world's first transparent game console, even going so far as to display that claim on the handheld's boot-up screen. While that might not be 100% true, given you can't see through every component that makes up the gadget, it's still an undeniably unique looking device. Along with its 1.51-inch 128 x 64 pixel resolution display, even the main PCB board and joystick buttons are translucent.

I've had the Arduview for a few weeks now, and it's just a joy to hold in my hand, or even to look at from across my desk.

I seriously can't get enough of this thing

The Arduview is easy to slip into a pocket and take on the go

The main draw here beyond the cool-looking design is the translucent 1.51-inch display. It's obviously super low resolution, but the pre-installed games are simple enough that they feel right at home on the miniscule screen. It's also easy to see in various lighting conditions, despite being mostly see-through, which surprised me. There's a thin line of what appears to be adhesive near the bottom of the display that I found distracting, so I hope this gets removed in the final version of the handheld (I was sent a pre-release build).

It's also worth noting that all the visuals are blue, in the same way that Nintendo's ill-fated Virtual Boy outputs entirely red graphics. I think this looks kind of cool and that it makes games pop in a unique way on the Arduview's translucent display, but I can see some people taking issue with the lack of any color.

Other key specs include an 8-bit ATmega32U4 chip, a 120mAh battery, and a USB-C port for charging. There's no 3.5mm audio jack, but there will be a built-in speaker (it didn't work on the pre-production unit Arduview sent me). The tiny handheld also weighs just 0.1lb (50g) and is roughly the size of a credit card, making it easy to slide into my pocket and take on the go. Overall, it's just a really cute-looking handheld.

On the game side, the Arduview features the same built-in titles as the Arduboy, a more traditional handheld that looks like a Game Boy. Most of the 300 games are pretty simple, which makes sense given the handheld's small screen and limited hardware power, but a few have actually caught my attention in a way I didn't expect.

ModRetro’s new transparent Chromatic Game Boy looks like it came straight out of the 2000s

The new see-through Chromatic is undeniably eye-catching.

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

The built-in games are simple time killers

Don't expect to find deep video game experience on the Arduview

First, there's Hopper, a game played from an up-down perspective that has you jumping between what seems to be trampolines. There are also more traditional platformers like The Crawl, which features a surprising amount of detail for such a small screen, along with snappy controls. Other games like Circuit Dude are homebrew takes on known arcade-style games like Chip's Challenge. The games I've tried so far are pretty surface-level, but they're fun for killing time and have actually kept me from doomscrolling on my phone a little less.

One key issue I've encountered so far is that the Arduview's buttons don't feel great. They're loud, stiff, and surprisingly inaccurate. I'm hoping this gets fixed before the final version of the handheld ships to buyers, because it would definitely get me using it more. The team behind the project says they're working on improving the buttons before the handheld ships to backers.

The Arduview is currently available on Kickstarter for $74 with early-bird pricing, with a retail price of $149. The campaign has raised $38,600, and it ends on December 8th.

The M64 reminds me why I love the Nintendo 64, flaws and all

If you're looking for an authentic way to play your Nintendo 64 cartridges, the M64 might soon be the best way to do it.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: A 3D-printed wall with 3,000 accessories turned my messy office into something I actually like
item.itunes:title: A 3D-printed wall with 3,000 accessories turned my messy office into something I actually like
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My favorite thing about 3D printing is creating useful stuff. Most of what I print winds up right in my office, helping me organize tools and equipment I’ve collected over the years. Perhaps my favorite organizational system of all is the Honeycomb Storage Wall (HSW).

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The concept is simple: take stuff you have lying around or in a drawer and hang it on the wall. Additionally, anything you might hang on a pegboard, you can hang on a HSW.

It’s lightweight and strong, modular and flexible. And there are over 3,000 accessories for it, including one design by yours truly.

Printing the Honeycomb Storage Wall

Take your time and measure

Printing the HSW is easy. There are several sizes made to fit the beds of common printers. The only caveat is you must use PETG filament to take advantage of its flexibility. Accessories (the things that fit into the wall) can be PLA or other plastic, but the wall itself must flex to allow inserts to snap into it.

I recommend measuring the space where you want to put the wall first, and then you can decide how many wall modules to print based on your dimensions. You’ll also need screw inserts to secure it to your wall. These snap into the HSW and provide a hole for you to screw it securely into your wall. Other inserts attach wall pieces together, so you can build the whole HSW on the floor and then attach it to your wall in one piece. When you attach your HSW, be sure to use at least one screw per attachment so it stays securely attached to your wall.

The fun begins when your wall is up and level, and it’s time to decide how you’ll de-clutter.

5 storage solutions you can 3D print for your home office

Clear the table clutter

1
By  Sumukh Rao

Accessories, accessories, accessories!

You can be overwhelmed by the sheer number of inserts available

Next, line up the stuff you want to attach. This could be anything from tools—and the 3D printing hobby generates a lot of new tools and equipment—to supplies, routers/switches and wire, to whatever you have lying around on flat surfaces. There are hooks, drawers, shelves, custom mounts, screwdriver holders, holders for pliers, wire crimpers, multimeters, and the list is so huge I could never summarize it all. The sky really is the limit: some great examples are a dog grooming wall, an entire wall of Game Boy cartridges, and a modular shelving system.

So head over to the remixes page on Printables. Thankfully, there is a search to help you narrow down what you want. Search by what you want to mount to the wall or by the type of mount it is (hook, drawer, shelf, etc.). Or just browse. You’ll be amazed at the variety of inserts there are.

The fit is snug

But the snap is glorious

One difference between the HSW and a standard pegboard is it’s not that easy to move things around on it once you’ve fastened them. Inserts snap into the wall with a satisfying click sound, and then they’re there to stay. If you want to remove an insert, you can use a flat screwdriver (or there’s a removal tool that sometimes works), but you’re certainly not going to adjust and readjust things very quickly.

The reason I say the removal tool sometimes works is that a lot of designers chose to add the insert instead of the hex shape that fits into the insert to their designs. This makes them snap into the wall directly, but it also makes them harder to move. The inserts were a key design choice for the HSW, and what makes it work like a pegboard. You print as many inserts as you need, and then you attach an accessory to the insert.

You can then pull the accessory out and move it easily. If you want to move the accessory, you print more inserts and put them into the wall where you want the accessory. This way, you reduce printing time for the wall itself, as it would take much longer to print if the inserts were built in.

A lot of designers chose to build the insert directly into their accessory, which means it snaps in, and then it doesn’t easily come out. If you are thinking about a design for the HSW, please don’t add the insert to your design. It wasn’t meant to work that way, and it makes it difficult to move accessories around.

How I used the Honeycomb Storage Wall

Is there another word for eclectic?

As my foray into the 3D printing hobby turned into a full-on stride, I started collecting a lot of tools and equipment. Nozzles, hot-ends, extruders, screws, fans, and so much filament. I also printed a lot of things: wire chains, drawer systems, spool holders, new cooling systems that were supposed to be more efficient, and more. As all this stuff proliferated, my office got really cluttered really fast.

When I found the HSW, I looked at my bare walls and said, “That’s it!” I already had a pegboard in my garage, so I could immediately see the application for my office—and I could print the wall instead of buying another pegboard. I now have Honeycomb Storage Walls holding whiteboard markers and an eraser, a remote for my mini-split, networking equipment and wire management in my office and basement, tool storage in my office, keyboard and headphone storage in my office, and spool storage for my 3D printing hobby. It’s reduced a ton of clutter, and I’m happy with it.

Alternatives to the Honeycomb Storage Wall

The wheel is constantly reinvented

Though the HSW came out first, there have been plenty of others who have created similar models:

  • Multibuild (formerly known as Multiboard): Rather than hexagons, the Multiboard is octagons, but the idea is similar. Enhancements include snappable and threadable accessories, so they’re easier to put in and take out. It’s offered under a commercial license, so you may not be able to download all accessories freely.
  • openGrid: This uses rounded squares and snappable mounts similar to the HSW. It’s a completely open design that might have been more popular if it had come out first. You should definitely check it out, though, especially as it boasts compatibility with Gridfinity and uses Multiconnect for accessories.
  • Thread Boards: Instead of hexagons, octagons, or squares, Thread Boards simplify things by having all accessories screw directly into the board. This makes them easily movable around the board. They give you a starter pack for free, but this is also offered under a commercial license, and most of the accessories are not free. This is a strong board, appropriate for heavy commercial tools.
  • GOEWS: Stands for the Greatly Over-Engineered Wall System. This is completely open source and available for modification in multiple formats (Fusion 360, openSCAD, and FreeCAD). Probably the strongest of all of these printable walls, it’s also most like a pegboard, as accessories are easily added and removed. While it doesn’t have many accessories, it makes up for that with online parts and accessories builders.

Decluttering reduces your stress

Regardless of which system you use, decluttering your environment is a good thing. Consider printing one of these and getting that stuff off of your flat surfaces and up on the wall. As for me, I’m sticking with the Honeycomb Storage Wall. It offers the best balance of strength and functionality, not to mention openness and variety of accessories. They will probably continue to multiply around my house, because though I quest for cleanliness and organization, it seems like I’ll always be striving for an unreachable goal.

The HSW is one tool that’s helping me get ever closer. I’ll make it, one day.

How I used the Honeycomb Storage Wall

Is there another word for eclectic?

As my foray into the 3D printing hobby turned into a full-on stride, I started collecting a lot of tools and equipment. Nozzles, hot-ends, extruders, screws, fans, and so much filament. I also printed a lot of things: wire chains, drawer systems, spool holders, new cooling systems that were supposed to be more efficient, and more. As all this stuff proliferated, my office got really cluttered really fast.

When I found the HSW, I looked at my bare walls and said, “That’s it!” I already had a pegboard in my garage, so I could immediately see the application for my office—and I could print the wall instead of buying another pegboard. I now have Honeycomb Storage Walls holding whiteboard markers and an eraser, a remote for my mini-split, networking equipment and wire management in my office and basement, tool storage in my office, keyboard and headphone storage in my office, and spool storage for my 3D printing hobby. It’s reduced a ton of clutter, and I’m happy with it.

The wheel is constantly reinvented

Though the HSW came out first, there have been plenty of others who have created similar models:

  • Multibuild (formerly known as Multiboard): Rather than hexagons, the Multiboard is octagons, but the idea is similar. It’s offered under a commercial license, so you may not be able to download all accessories freely.
  • openGrid: This uses rounded squares and snappable mounts similar to the HSW. It’s a completely open design that might have been more popular if it had come out first. You should definitely check it out, though, especially as it boasts compatibility with Gridfinity and uses Multiconnect for accessories.
  • Thread Boards: Instead of hexagons, octagons, or squares, Thread Boards simplify things by having all accessories screw directly into the board. This makes them easily movable around the board. They give you a starter pack for free, but this is also offered under a commercial license, and most of the accessories are not free. This is a strong board, appropriate for heavy commercial tools.
  • GOEWS: Stands for the Greatly Over-Engineered Wall System. This is completely open source and available for modification in multiple formats (Fusion 360, openSCAD, and FreeCAD). Probably the strongest of all of these printable walls, it’s also most like a pegboard, as accessories are easily added and removed. While it doesn’t have many accessories, it makes up for that with online parts and accessories builders.

Decluttering reduces your stress

Regardless of which system you use, decluttering your environment is a good thing. Consider printing one of these and getting that stuff off of your flat surfaces and up on the wall. As for me, I’m sticking with the Honeycomb Storage Wall. It offers the best balance of strength and functionality, not to mention openness and variety of accessories. They will probably continue to multiply around my house, because though I quest for cleanliness and organization, it seems like I’ll always be striving for an unreachable goal.

The HSW is one tool that’s helping me get ever closer. I’ll make it, one day.

item.itunes:title: Which open source office suite is right for you? LibreOffice, Collabora, or Nextcloud
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Office suites were exciting in the 90s because there was competition. You had your Corel/WordPerfect stalwarts (mostly lawyers), your IBM-centric Lotus SmartSuite users, and of course you had Microsoft, which slowly chipped away at everybody’s market share until Office became the de facto standard. After that, office suites became kind of a boring wait for the next version of Microsoft Office. With no real competition, Office became so expensive that Sun Microsystems found it more economical to buy Star Division to obtain StarOffice (which they renamed OpenOffice) than it would have been to license Microsoft Office for their users. Since then, we’ve mostly had two camps: Microsoft Office on Windows and Mac, and LibreOffice (what OpenOffice became) on Linux, Windows, and Mac.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

But now things are changing, and office suite competition is heating up. People are tired of renting their software by shelling out for a subscription to Microsoft Office every year. And new open source alternatives are available. Of course, there’s the venerable LibreOffice. But now Collabora Office and Nextcloud Office have entered the fray: both of which promise a similar experience to those coming from Microsoft Office, along with enhanced compatibility with Microsoft’s formats. But which one should you choose? That, my friend, depends on your needs. Read on for a closer look.

LibreOffice: old faithful

Sometimes what’s familiar is what’s best

LibreOffice is still installed by default on most Linux distributions. If you’ve been using Linux for a long time as I have, LibreOffice may have become your familiar friend for creating documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. And if you’re a Windows or Mac user who gave up on paying for an office suite subscription a long time ago, you probably have LibreOffice installed on your machine.

For those not in the know, LibreOffice contains six programs: Writer (word processor), Calc (spreadsheet), Impress (presentations), Draw (vector graphics), Base (database), and Math (formulas). Each component is highly competent at what it does; I have done extensive diagrams with Draw and laid out entire books with Writer, complete with an index and a table of contents.

You should be aware of one thing with regard to LibreOffice: its default file formats are the OpenDocument file formats, not the Microsoft Office formats. While it boasts high compatibility with the Microsoft formats, if your primary purpose with your office suite is to share files with people who use Microsoft Office, LibreOffice might not be for you. It will not default to Microsoft formats, though it can save them.

Now, when I say high compatibility, I do mean it. I was able to use LibreOffice on Linux along with its track changes feature to collaborate with my editor on a book, chapter by chapter — and this was over 15 years ago. She never complained of any problems, and neither did the layout people. When I read LibreOffice reviews that doubt its compatibility with Microsoft formats, I’m always puzzled by this, because I’ve had very few problems doing that, for a long time.

As Microsoft kills off Publisher, LibreOffice steps in with free support for your PUB files

No need to convert them.

11
By  Simon Batt

One thing I love about LibreOffice (at least on Linux) is that its default interface does not use ribbons. This is another area in which you may be different from me, especially if you are used to Microsoft Office. If I use a piece of software for a long time, I want to learn the keyboard shortcuts. Ribbons force me to grab the mouse instead, and they don’t show the relevant keyboard shortcuts so I can learn them. And they take up too much space. And I have to read hieroglyphics (i.e., icons) to know what the functions do.

With that said, LibreOffice does offer a ribbon: if you don’t like the pull-down menus, you can select View -> User Interface and select the tabbed option.

LibreOffice is likely the best suite for those who only occasionally have to deal with Microsoft formats (not because of compatibility, but because they’re not the default), or those who have been using it for a while. It’s powerful, stable, and for those familiar with it, there’s little reason to switch.

Collabora Office

Supported, cross-platform LibreOffice you can run locally or online

Collabora Office runs from the same code base as LibreOffice. In fact, Collabora is the biggest contributor to LibreOffice. And it has the same six programs as LibreOffice. So why use Collabora when you could use LibreOffice?

Collabora’s main thing is the collaboration piece. Collabora Office runs in a browser, which means you get all those great features you may be used to from Google Docs: multiple users with multiple cursors modifying a document at the same time — and talking to each other about it in chat. Collabora also uses the ribbon interface by default, so it’s a more familiar environment for Microsoft Office users. If, however, you’re used to Google Docs (which has pull-down menus), you may want to go to the View tab and select Compact view to get pull-down menus like Google Docs.

Collabora is a great alternative to Microsoft 365. You can adopt Collabora for your organization by signing up for an account. Or you can use it within a Nextcloud installation. Or you can even install a standalone version that doesn’t have an online component. This works slightly differently from LibreOffice, in that all the office components are embedded in a single window, and files appear in tabs across the top.

Collabora Office shines within organizations that have a Collabora account or a Nextcloud instance and work on documents together.

Nextcloud Office

Once written, twice forked

Nextcloud Office is the youngest suite in this roundup. It’s a fork of Euro-Office, which itself is a fork of OnlyOffice, a dual-licensed (commercial and Affero GPL) office suite designed for online and offline use.

Because it is also built for online collaboration, it runs in a browser. The standalone version of Nextcloud Office by default also runs all of its components in a single window, with files in tabs across the top, though there is a setting to open them in separate windows. It uses a ribbon interface similar to Microsoft Office. In fact, it is designed to be as similar to Microsoft Office as possible, matching the functions and organization of its interface closely. There is no way to switch this interface to a pull-down menu interface.

The standalone version of Nextcloud Office comes with four programs: Nextcloud Write, Nextcloud Spreadsheet, Nextcloud Present, and Nextcloud PDF Editor. I tested the word processor with the biggest document I could find: a public domain Bible in .docx format. I loaded it up and tried one change: modify the default style’s font and see if Nextcloud’s word processor could reformat almost 2000 pages. Unfortunately, I got the error you see above. This test worked in LibreOffice and Collabora Office.

Nextcloud Office’s default file format is all the Microsoft formats, so it is positioned as a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Office. I threw a bunch of files at it, and it formatted all the Microsoft files well. If you are coming from LibreOffice, however, its OpenDocument support seems lacking; I had problems with several of my complex files.

Perhaps the pièce de rèsistance for Nextcloud Office is its integration with Nextcloud. Like with Collabora, if you are looking for a replacement for Microsoft 365 or Google Drive accounts and need real-time online collaboration, combining Nextcloud with Nextcloud Office could be exactly what you need. Because its default format is the ooxml format Microsoft Office uses, you should be able to migrate all your files from OneDrive to a Nextcloud instance and have your users collaborate on files almost the same way they did before.

Office suites are exciting again

Who had this on their bingo card?

After about two decades of one dominant (and boring) office suite, we now have several viable, open-source options. You should take each one for a test drive and see how it handles your existing files. And if you are building an environment where users collaborate on documents, you don’t have to accept the default suite and its default pricing: you have several options available to you — including hosting Nextcloud on your own hardware for free.

Give one of these suites a try!

item.title: A smart plug showed my home lab wasted a lot of power, and the worst offenders surprised me
item.itunes:title: A smart plug showed my home lab wasted a lot of power, and the worst offenders surprised me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
After connecting a smart energy monitoring plug to my always-on home lab and discovering that the idle power draw was slightly higher and more expensive than I expected, I wanted to test alternatives (to see if I could bring down that continuous consumption). My home lab was consuming 12.1 kWh of electricity per week, totaling 630.7 kWh of electricity per year. Based on the U.S. average residential electricity price of 18.16 cents per kWh, this would mean my home lab cost me over $100 per year in electricity, or roughly $9.50 per month (a monthly subscription cost I'd think twice about).

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Some of the changes I tried made no difference, but here are the adjustments that actually reduced idle draw in testing without sacrificing any of my core lab reliability.

I plugged my whole home lab into a smart energy monitoring plug for a week, and the electric bill reality check shocked me

Even idle power draw adds up significantly.

By  Jasmine Mannan

Opting for a plug felt like the most accurate measurement method

I needed to trim extra hardware

The reason I opted for a smart energy monitoring plug, as opposed to internal OS telemetry, is that a wall outlet reveals true continuous draw in watts and cumulative kilowatt-hours (including AC-to-DC adapter inefficiencies). Some consumer smart plugs vary in measurement accuracy, especially at very low wattages or with non-linear power supplies, so I treated my readings as practical baselines rather than a laboratory calibration.

I did firsthand checks across my always-on compute, storage, and networking gear. This included a mini PC, my NAS, and switches. They sit mostly idle between scheduled tasks or background jobs. By consolidating light workloads or powering down secondary devices during off-hours, I was able to remove fixed baseline draw that runs every hour of the year.

Spinning hard drive disks can consume noticeable idle power compared to solid-state drives, so I ensure I spin down my idle mechanical drives. I configured the specific spin-down timeouts where workload tolerates brief wake-up latency, lowering idle draw. However, keep in mind when doing this that frequent spin-ups can add wear, so very short timeouts can shorten your drive life.

Alongside this, disconnecting any unused USB peripherals, monitors, or display outputs when running headless is another fundamental change to make if you're hoping to reduce your power consumption (as active display controllers or peripherals can prevent systems from dropping into deeper low-power states, as well as consuming a lot of power themselves even when in standby).

Auditing my CPU C-states gave me valuable insight

Background containers can cause issues

Modern x86 processors save substantial idle power by entering deeper CPU idle states, sometimes referred to as C-states, when cores are unused, whereas a performance CPU frequency governor or misconfigured power profile can keep clock speeds elevated unnecessarily. By using standard Linux diagnostic tools like powertop, I was able to inspect C-state residency, device wakeups, and thermal-tunable kernel parameters.

You have to be wary when it comes to tuning, as forcing overly restrictive governors or aggressive auto-suspend on every single device can actually introduce wake-up latency. As a result, it can interfere with network interfaces or cause instability on specific motherboards or kernel versions. You should always test any changes that you're making incrementally and verify stability under normal lab load rather than applying blind scripts and walking away.

Also, keep an eye on background containers, monitoring agents, or scripts polling APIs and logs every few seconds, as these can repeatedly wake the CPU from deep idle states. You can adjust polling intervals where real-time granularity isn't actually needed or stop or schedule non-essential containers instead of leaving every experiment running 24/7. This can reduce that background CPU wake-up without breaking any of your core services.

My cameras were the worst offenders

PoE switches might need reconsidering

Another thing I was sure to do was reevaluate my switch and PoE port power because managed switches and power-over-Ethernet gear carry a baseline operational draw even when connected clients are quiet and unused. By disabling unused ports or turning off PoE on ports feeding devices that don't require it, you can shave off modest continuous watts. Personally, I ended up sticking to my PoE cameras as it's what works best for me, but just switching off one camera temporarily did bring down my consumption by 10W.

It might be worth matching your link speeds and power-saving features to the actual needs of your devices. A lot of multi-gigabit or 10 GBE links, especially copper RJ45 transceivers, generally draw more power than gigabit links or short-range direct attach cables, depending on the hardware design. If your devices only need 1 Gbps or can safely use Link Power Management/Energy Efficient Ethernet without causing packet drops or latency spikes, it might be worth making the switch. But verify the behavior empirically rather than assuming zero trade-offs because this isn't always the case.

Some of the biggest power consumers in my always-on home lab were my camera setups, where continuous recording, frequent motion processing, or cloud-dependent polling can keep the devices active. I switched from always-on streaming to event-driven capture, and it allowed my cameras to drop down to idle states more frequently, saving me power, but in turn, you don't always have a continuous stream. You have to make sure that your camera is sensitive enough to capture everything you want it to.

Small changes can make a large difference

item.title: The leading unofficial GTA 6 PC port vanished from GitHub just as it reached a playable 25-30fps
item.itunes:title: The leading unofficial GTA 6 PC port vanished from GitHub just as it reached a playable 25-30fps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Just as CGBJ, one of the leading unofficial GTA 6 PC ports, reportedly hit a playable 25-30fps, its GitHub page mysteriously disappeared just minutes after going public. It's unclear whether the team behind the project made it private to avoid a potential takedown notice, or whether Rockstar's legal department hit the project and its related repositories with a DMCA.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It usually takes at least a few days for GitHub DMCA takedown notices to be publicly available. When you try to navigate to CGBJ's GitHub page, it currently returns a 404 error. Several forks of the project are still active, so the team behind CGBJ may have pulled it down themselves.

Earlier this week, Rockstar's parent company Take-Two Interactive took down Leonida, one of the leading GTA 6 PC ports, and its 3,007 associated repositories with a DMCA takedown, though its 15-year-old creator is already teasing a comeback.

Over the past few days, various unofficial GTA 6 PC port projects have appeared, with projects like VIctory, Belobug, and CGBJ (which at one point was private) leading the pack, according to PortwatchVI, a website tracking the progress of these fan-made ports. Just yesterday, Belobug hit 5-7fps, so CGBJ hitting 25-30fps a few hours later is an impressive achievement.

All of these GTA 6 ports are based on a leaked copy of the Xbox version of the game that appeared online earlier this week courtesy of Cyberleek, the same individual or group behind leaks surrounding the game from earlier this year. Cyberleek first released the game's files, followed by the executable required for developers to get to work on porting the Xbox version to PC.

Unofficial GTA 6 PC ports are improving at a staggering pace

The PS5 version of GTA 6 has also reportedly leaked online

Credit: Rockstar

Since the Xbox Series X/S and most Windows gaming PCs share the same x86-64 CPU architecture, projects like CGBJ can run much of GTA 6's code without recompiling it. The project, which is actually a fork of VIctory, uses a hybrid compatibility layer that combines VIctory's runtime with XCL's shader translation technology. That said, Xbox-specific dependencies need to be recreated, and graphics have to be translated so a Windows PC can understand them. An Nvidia RTX 5090 (16GB of VRAM) was reportedly used in CGBJ's testing.

The PS5 version of GTA 6 has also reportedly leaked, opening up more options for developers working on unofficial PC ports. The work is still in the early stages, but reports indicate the game is already booting in the KytyPS5 emulator.

While GTA 6 is now available on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, Rockstar hasn't announced an official PC version yet. Rumors point to an official PC version of GTA 6 launching somewhere between six months and a year from now. It's possible that the relentless efforts to unofficially bring the game to PC will encourage Rockstar to launch the port it's definitely working on but still hasn't revealed, at least a bit earlier.

GTA 6 is already running at 60fps with DLSS 5 with the help of a PC, thanks to a clever PS5 Remote Play workaround

This one is for all the PC gamers out there raging over the console-exclusive's 30fps

By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: 5 things Xbox’s couch mode needs to copy from SteamOS
item.itunes:title: 5 things Xbox’s couch mode needs to copy from SteamOS
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Being able to pick up a controller, sit down on the couch, and immediately start playing games is seen by many as a console-exclusive experience, but it really doesn't have to be. SteamOS and Steam Big Picture are proof of that, and when using them I can easily leave the keyboard and mouse stowed away.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

As someone who has a home theater PC in their living room and uses it almost every day, I'm constantly hunting for new ways to make the experience more seamless, but when I swapped it back to Windows and tried the "Xbox Mode" that came with it, it left a lot to be desired. While it's certainly more than just a full-screen skin for the Xbox app, it falls short of Steam Big Picture and SteamOS in a lot of key areas, and these 5 features are what Microsoft should be copying from Valve.

I've been running SteamOS on a non-Steam mini PC, and it makes a better living room console than I expected

Steam makes great gaming experiences.

1
By  Rich Edmonds

It needs to stop sending me to the desktop

Steam is great at minimizing this

A "couch mode" really only works if you never have to pull out a mouse to navigate. SteamOS's Gameing Mode runs games inside its own compositor called gamescope, and that means anything that pops up before the game launches, like a EULA acceptance or anti-cheat launcher can be navigated properly. Steam Input has a lot to do with this too, but one of the biggest reasons why these sorts of windows are such a hurdle for couch gaming on Windows is because the Xbox environment isn't completely separate like gamescope.

Xbox Mode is just a controller-friendly shell on top of regular Windows, and while you can launch basically anything directly from the interface, it's a different story once it's running. Valve also went so far as to make this a requirement to be "Verified" for the Steam Deck: if a game launched something that isn't navigable using a controller, it displays a compatibility warning on the store page. My couch PC isn't a handheld, but the warnings hold up all the same.

I built a Steam Machine out of spare PC parts and you can, too

If you have old PC hardware lying around or an aging Windows laptop, you might be able to breathe new life into it with SteamOS

2
By  Stevie Bonifield

Remapping that works for every controller, in every game

Steam Input is one of my favorite things about Steam

Steam Input is one of the biggest reasons why SteamOS and Steam Big Picture feel so seamless from the couch. Almost every game has a controller layout by default, and community configs are at your fingertips. Support for features like gyro, back button mapping, keyboard and mouse emulation, and plug-and-play support for most controllers is really useful.

Microsoft's button remapping requires the use of the Xbox Accessories app, and most of what you can do there requires an Xbox controller. To be fair to Microsoft, Steam Input does work on Windows, but only on games that are launched through Steam. Xbox's own games launched through Game Pass or the Microsoft Store can't use Steam Input, so you're stuck using the inferior option.

How I turned my gaming PC into the ultimate console at home

PC gaming isn't always streamlined, but we can fix that.

15
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A quick menu for performance

It's a bit barebones on Windows at the moment

With a couple of button presses on any game launched through SteamOS or Steam Big Picture, you can pull up the Performance tab, which grants you quick access to several settings and overlay options, all of which can be applied on a per-game basis with profiles. The Xbox equivalent, the Performance widget on the Game Bar, lets you track resource utilization and display statistics, but per-game settings don't exist. You can apply per-game settings like frame limiters in the Nvidia App or AMD Adrenalin, but there's no way to easily toggle them through a controller-friendly menu.

Microsoft might finally get me to use Xbox Game Bar with its latest update

Oh, that thing?

By  Jacob Roach

Suspend and resume capability that you don't have to think about

A true console-esque feature

SteamOS treats suspend and resume as a core feature, and it's really useful, even on a full-sized PC. Pressing the power button in the middle of a game will suspend the system, and when waking it later, you'll pick up right where you left off with nothing to relaunch.

Waking a Windows PC with a controller is far from straightforward—it's possible with the right BIOS settings and some PowerShell tweaks, but it'd be a lot nicer if it was just a simple toggle by default. The frustrating part is that Microsoft already solved this with Quick Resume on the Series X and S, so the bones are there.

I installed Bazzite on the Steam Deck, and I regret it

I tried it, so you don't have to.

19
By  Joe Rice-Jones

One place for every update

They won't do it, but a custom Xbox image would be great

SteamOS installs and updates as a single image, and that means the kernel, graphics driver, firmware, and basically everything else comes from one system update, including fallback measures if something were to go wrong. Keeping a Windows PC current means updating all of these elements individually: Windows Update, the Microsoft Store, Gaming Services, the Xbox app and whatever GPU utility your card needs.

Microsoft knows that this is a problem, since it seems to be one of the core selling points of Project Helix, their hybrid PC-Xbox machine that has been in the works for the last few years. With the release of Helix, if they enabled the ability for users install a SteamOS-like operating system on their own PCs that could primarily function as the base for a couch gaming box, that would be great, but it's unlikely. At the minimum, I'd love to see a more streamlined update system for Windows machines that want to be used from the couch.

I won't use anything but Steam for PC gaming because of this one feature

I primarily play games through Steam for this single reason.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

Windows has strengths, but the Xbox Mode is a bit of an afterthought

Windows already has the game library and access to Microsoft's other services, but it lacks the unglamorous plumbing that makes SteamOS feel effortless from the couch: controllers that just work, games that sleep when you do, and updates you never think about. Valve built that layer over years of Steam Deck updates, and I hope Microsoft takes Helix in a similar direction.

item.title: I replaced YouTube's app with OpenTubeX and its self-hosted backend, and I don't want to go back
item.itunes:title: I replaced YouTube's app with OpenTubeX and its self-hosted backend, and I don't want to go back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As Google's desire to maximize revenue from YouTube grows, the user experience arguably gets worse. Ads are more intrusive than ever, and the service pushes its most popular channels, which are often riddled with low-effort content and so-called "AI slop". So what if you could make YouTube into a more peaceful experience without sacrificing some of the things you love about it?

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That's where OpenTubeX comes in. I'd heard of a few YouTube clients before this, but OpenTubeX only recently crossed my radar, and I already regret not knowing about it sooner. It may just be the best way to use YouTube if you want a more peaceful experience.

A YouTube experience tailored to me

It's heavily customizable

Right off the bat, OpenTubeX sells itself by just letting you tailor your experience to your specific wants or needs. Instead of making assumptions about what you want to see, the initial setup asks you to choose the default video quality (which it actually sticks to), whether to show captions by default, the default landing page for the app, and which region trending content should be pulled from.

On top of that, it asks me if I want to enable SponsorBlock (for skipping sponsored segments in videos) as well as another service I'd never heard of called DeArrow. The idea is that many clickbait-y YouTube videos rely on big red arrows in the thumbnail, so DeArrow is meant to remove the clickbait aspects of these videos. It can also be applied to titles, so misleading or sensationalist titles are replaced with community-provided ones that are (presumably) more honest.

In the app's settings, you'll actually find a couple more add-ons, including AiSList, a community-maintained list of videos and channels that rely on AI slop. This filters those videos out of recommendations, searches, and the trending page, and adds warnings to channels flagged by the service. The famed Return YouTube Dislike service is also available, so you can see a video's dislike count.

I set up Jellyfin for movies, but YouTube videos became the real reason I use it

It takes some work, but it's worth it

3
By  João Carrasqueira

One thing I also like about OpenTubeX is that the Home page is almost entirely based on your watch history. If you want to see trending videos, there's a dedicated tab for it, but your home page includes things such as a Continue Watching section for videos you previously started watching, a section for new videos from your subscriptions, and recommendations based on your watch history. There are no sneaky algorithms at play here, which I love.

It's faster than I expected

And very fully featured

OpenTubeX isn't the first third-party YouTube client I try, and with some of the others I've used in the past, the experience felt more like a compromise. The UI wasn't always as fast as I'd like, and loading a video could be especially problematic. I think back to options like NewPipe on Android or FreeTube on Linux, and I'm not exactly eager to use them again.

OpenTubeX is a different story. The UI feels designed much more purposefully, and everything is very smooth. Navigating the app feels great (though the animation for viewing open tabs on Android feels a little off), and it's very responsive. Loading videos, too, seems faster than I expected going in. It is a bit slower than using the official YouTube app on my phone, but it seems to be hardware-dependent. My desktop PC feels no slower than the YouTube website.

You still get most of the features you'd want, too, and they look about as good as you could hope for. Closed captions are here, likes and dislikes are visible — though you can't like or dislike a video yourself, since you'd need a YouTube account for that — and comments are visible with comment threads, likes, and creator reactions all working. There are even some features here the official app doesn't offer, like the ability to see a transcript next to the video, including the ability to download it. It's really cool.

And if you go into the app's settings, there's a ton to play around with to tailor the app to your liking. From things as simple as UI scaling, to disabling comments and recommended videos on the video page, theming options, seek bar behaviors, tabs, playback settings, and so much more. I couldn't possibly cover it all here, but this app is anything but undercooked.

It's not just YouTube, either

Other video platforms also work

It's not obvious at first glance, but if you look into OpenTubeX's settings, you'll also find the option to follow channels that aren't on YouTube. In fact, the app supports a decent range of other media sites, including Twitch, SoundCloud, and a couple others. For Twitch, you can watch replays from a specific channel, and it even supports live chat replays, so you can see what viewers were saying during a stream. OpenTubeX can also notify you if a channel you follow is live.

For platforms that aren't officially supported, you can also add RSS feeds so you can get content from a specific creator or website. OpenTubeX can display RSS feed items from any source, but they won't actually load unless there's a video stream that can be pulled using yt-dlp, so it's still meant for video content.

You can stay in sync without Google

On most devices, anyway

The big drawback with many of the YouTube clients I've tried in the past is that they're not really designed to sync across devices. Options like NewPipe and FreeTube all take pride in storing data locally, but that means you can't really carry your experience across devices. OpenTubeX addresses this with its own self-hosted sync server, based on a similar service called LibreTube but with more capabilities focused on OpenTubeX features.

You can deploy the OpenTubeX server relatively easily using a Docker compose file, and then connect to it on the local network or set up a reverse proxy to connect to it remotely. I wish there was a Proxmox community script for the service, but I deployed it using Docker on my Windows laptop (after struggling with Docker for a good while), and it worked about as well as I could have hoped. I did most of my setup on my PC, but this also let me easily bring my content over to my phone.

There is also a public sync server if you're okay with syncing data to the cloud. Plus, you can sign in with a proper YouTube account, though the app warns this could result in your account being banned or deleted for using unofficial apps, and I would advise against it.

OpenTubeX is amazing

While I've been drawn to unofficial YouTube apps before, none of them have ever truly stuck with me because they often have annoying limitations. But with OpenTubeX, I may actually be willing to switch and use the app full-time. Between the great overall feel of the app and the fact that I can finally sync my data, it's the most tempting option yet. I highly recommend checking it out for yourself.

OpenTubeX

item.itunes:title: A home NAS doesn't need 10GbE, these are the 3 things I'd spend that money on first
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Upgrading a NAS with 10-gigabit Ethernet requires matching hardware across the entire data path, from switches, network cards or adapters, cabling or transceivers, and client endpoints, which quickly drives up cost and power draw. In practical home workloads such as media streaming, routine backups, container hosting, and multi-drive hard disk drive arrays, mechanical drive speeds, protocol overhead, encryption, or client interfaces frequently cap throughput well below 10Gbps even when a 10GbE link is present.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For most home setups where a 1GbE or 2.5GbE link is already in place, putting that budget into storage capacity/flash caching, memory and compute headroom, and resilient backup architecture typically gives you more noticeable day-to-day improvements rather than chasing peak link speed.

I connected my NAS directly to my PC with 10 gigabit Ethernet, and skipped upgrading the rest of my network

You don't necessarily need a 10G switch to get blazing-fast transfer speeds between your PC and NAS

13
By  Ayush Pande

More drives are a great addition

Whether it's to expand storage or increase speeds

Drives are likely throttling your network first, so investing in an SSD could be a better upgrade for you. A typical smaller spinning hard drive array used for bulk home storage likely cannot sustain sequential read/write rates anywhere near 10Gbps, which roughly caps out at 1,250MB/s at a theoretical max before considering any overhead, let alone random I/O for small files or virtual machine images. As a result, a 10GbE connection often sits idle waiting on platters.

A flash pool could make a major difference to your setup. Adding an M.2 NVMe solid-state drive as a read-write cache or dedicated flash pool can accelerate media metadata lookups, small file transfers, container databases, and bursty writes. Of course, your real-world gains will depend on your workload patterns and whether the NAS has enough PCIe lanes and CPU headroom to feed the drives.

If you're hoping to increase your raw capacity, then picking up more HDDs can be a solid investment. Whether that's buying larger-capacity drives or moving from a single-drive setup (such as a non-RAID personal storage appliance) to a redundant multi-drive array, it addresses practical storage limits and drive failure tolerance immediately, whereas 10GbE does nothing when you run out of terabytes.

Upgrading a workstation and NAS to 10GbE, factoring in a multi-port switch or SFP+ transceiver, network interface cards or Thunderbolt adapters, and Cat6a/fiber runs, can easily cost you several hundred dollars: money that can go directly towards extra terabytes of storage or NVMe drives.

Higher compute is a great investment

Invest in your specifications

The specifications of your NAS system itself are also likely a better investment when compared to 10GbE. Compute and RAM matter before link speed does.

Home NAS boxes increasingly run Docker containers, media transcoding, file checksums, compression, snapshots, and encryption alongside file sharing. Low-power CPUs or tight RAM capacities on your NAS can bottleneck throughput, background maintenance tasks, and multi-service responsiveness long before a 2.5GbE link saturates.

Investing in extra RAM can improve your day-to-day performance because additional memory gives the operating system more room for file system caches and background services (reducing that disk thrashing during concurrent reads, writes, or scrub/indexing jobs, especially on systems that are running ZFS or heavy container stacks).

Backup protection

Whether it's a second backup site or cloud storage

Backup redundancy is something to always consider. RAID is not a backup. A redundant drive array protects uptime if a single drive fails, but it does not protect against accidental deletion, file corruption, ransomware, bad software updates, or physical damage to the NAS chassis.

Instead of investing in a 10GbE link, spending that money on a dedicated local backup target or offsite/cloud backup plan can directly reduce data loss risk.

Another level of protection you might want to invest in is an uninterruptible power supply. Sudden power flickers or outages during writes, RAID rebuilds, or file system metadata updates can cause file system errors or drive issues. item.title: 4 Docker containers I've never once had to fix, and they're the ones I'd tell any beginner to start with
item.itunes:title: 4 Docker containers I've never once had to fix, and they're the ones I'd tell any beginner to start with
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I started self-hosting by trying out individual apps, and the first one was easy. All it took was a few commands to set the whole thing up and access its web page via a browser. But as I matured in the DIY realm, Docker replaced individual packages. It became a central part of the workflow, and now tools live as individual containers rather than the old, individual approach. You might already be aware of the perks of this containerization approach, as it makes things more manageable.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

One tool's failure doesn't drag the whole system down, which is quite common while troubleshooting individual packages. But not all containers are as easygoing as you think. Some require frequent monitoring and maintenance, which can be overwhelming for a beginner. However, there are a few low-maintenance containers you can deploy on your home server.

OmniTools

Myriad of tools for everyday use

OmniTools is one of those containers that doesn't need any upkeep at all apart from periodic updates. It's a collection of multiple tools, over a hundred as per the current GitHub page’s summary. You might wonder why I need hundreds of tools, and whether it will require a huge chunk of storage space. Well, OmniTools isn't one of those resource-hungry, storage space-eating monsters that will stress your home server. It can work with less than 100MB of memory on low-spec SBCs.

I've deployed it on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W along with a couple of other lightweight tools, and they don't even utilize half of the available memory on the SBC. The magic lies in the nature of the operation because OmniTools is primarily a client-side processing service. It only hosts the core files on your server while the client's browser handles all the processing. The files that you upload and process aren't stored on the server.

I use these 5 tools to turn my Raspberry Pi into a self-hosting behemoth

Even a Raspberry Pi can become a containerization war machine with the right set of apps

By  Ayush Pande

I use it to batch convert images, remove backgrounds, and extract audio from videos and clips. It's a fast, feature-rich, and free experience that other freemium web-based tools rarely offer. Even other people in my home use it for day-to-day document conversions and image actions. It is just a browser search away for all the people connected to my home Wi-Fi. Since the first day of its deployment, I have never once had to fix the tool because it closed unexpectedly or didn't have the necessary permissions to work.

Vaultwarden

My local and private password manager

Self-hosting a password manager was the last thing on my mind, but it happened after the paid ones became expensive and unpredictable. Vaultwarden fit in very nicely, and it worked without issue both as a standalone package and a Docker container. I ran it as a standalone installation for about a year until one day I decided it was time to turn it into a container.

That opened a can of worms because I had to figure out HTTPS support as well, which eventually worked with the help of Tailscale Serve. Unlike OmniTools, Vaultwarden stores your credentials in a database on the server. There have been no database errors or problems while fetching credentials via the mobile application or the browser extension.

That said, Vaultwarden has a slightly more difficult setup compared to BentoPDF and OmniTools. But once you overcome the initial hiccups like HTTPS support, it doesn't feel different from a paid password manager. The autofill works well, and you can generate random yet powerful passwords and audit your existing ones.

BentoPDF

No more Adobe Acrobat

BentoPDF is one of the most beginner-friendly containers because PDF is a common file format for both students and working professionals. There's a lot of file conversion and PDF editing required in both roles, and BentoPDF acts as a free, self-hosted solution. Adobe Acrobat is more expensive than other PDF tools. BentoPDF only requires a one-time setup and server configuration. Like OmniTools, there's no heavy lifting done on the server, and the client side bears all the burden.

It also doesn't store or process the files on the server and doesn't use a database like Vaultwarden. So there are fewer moving parts, and you can deploy it once via a simple Docker Run command and use it immediately. Most of the features that I earlier used Adobe Acrobat for are now a part of the BentoPDF suite, so I hesitate to switch to another one.

4 essential Docker containers i run on every new server

A collection of handy containers to manage my workstations

9
By  Ayush Pande

I used Stirling PDF earlier, but it wasn't a great fit for low-spec SBCs like the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. After BentoPDF, I've stopped visiting free web PDF editors and converters because they serve a ton of ads and paywall the useful features. OmniTools also has a few PDF-related features, but I prefer to have a dedicated tool for PDF tasks.

Dockhand

A cleaner Portainer alternative

A beginner should not have to deal with the terminal for deploying and managing containers. A visual tool like Portainer makes both learning and management quite easy, and I prefer Dockhand. It’s a better alternative to Portainer, in my opinion, and adds a few features I wanted in Portainer.

Selective container updates are one of the features that convinced me to make the switch. You don’t need to bulk update all of them. Similarly, the visual style is much easier on the eyes and supports more customization than Portainer. The container-related actions are readily available in the list, and I can pause, restart, or run any stopped ones.

9 Docker containers that run 24/7 on my $100 mini PC

Maximum value budget homelab.

19
By  Samir Makwana

I also find the scheduled maintenance actions very supportive for mundane tasks. The built-in file browser feature makes adding files to a server’s media folder quite easy. The tool runs and manages every other container on my servers without acting finicky, and that means one less problem to worry about.

Choose containers wisely

The containers mentioned above have posed negligible hassles since the day I deployed them. Your experience can vary, and some of you might feel strongly about Nextcloud or Pi-Hole. These are incredibly useful tools, but I had a tough time with them as a beginner. Pi-Hole needs a bit more tinkering and can bring the network down if you don't have a fallback server.

Docker

Docker Desktop simplifies container management on Mac, Linux, or Windows with a GUI, handling setups like port mappings and file systems

item.title: Why frame generation needs 15% of your GPU left idle to actually feel smooth
item.itunes:title: Why frame generation needs 15% of your GPU left idle to actually feel smooth
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you crank your in-game graphics settings until your GPU hits 99% utilization, and then turn on Frame Generation to smooth out a heavy game, you aren't using it wrong. Instead, you are using the tech for the exact purpose it was built for: increasing displayed frame rates in a demanding game, with a possible trade-off in latency. The problem with this approach is that it can noticeably increase input lag and sometimes ruin the overall gaming experience.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

From my findings, there is another, rather unconventional way to use it that lowered input lag in my testing. Instead of letting my GPU sit at 99% load, I deliberately left some breathing room, around 15%. Rather than settling for the frame cap approach, I intentionally pushed my system to a CPU wall and used that bottleneck to my advantage. Even if your hardware pushes you toward a clean frame cap or a second GPU instead, leaving a slice of your card idle often makes those extra frames feel right.

The upside is remarkable, but the cost isn't equal for all.
